title: Comparative assessment of OPC and portland composite cements on the rheology and strength of nylon fiber-modified self-compacting concrete
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the combined effects of Portland composite cement type and nylon fiber dosage on the fresh-property compliance and 28-day mechanical performance of self-compacting concrete (SCC). An empirical SCC proportioning approach was adopted. Four OPC-based trial mixes were first evaluated using slump flow diameter, t500, V-funnel, L-box, and visual stability criteria in accordance with EN 12350, ACI 237R-07, and JSCE guidelines, from which an optimally balanced SCC mixture was selected as the baseline. Using this reference mix, two composite cements (CEM II/A-M and CEM II/B-M) were investigated with nylon fiber contents of 0, 0.1, 0.25, and 0.5%. Fresh results show that increasing fiber content reduces slump flow and passing ability and increases flow resistance, confirming a workability–toughness trade-off; SCC compliance remained reliable up to ~ 0.25% fiber, while 0.5% approached or exceeded fresh-property limits in CEM II/A-M and remained borderline acceptable in CEM II/B-M. Under constant w/c and admixture dosage, higher SCM composite cement improved rheology and passing ability (CEM II/B-M > CEM II/A-M > OPC) but reduced 28-day strength, following clinker content (OPC > CEM II/A-M > CEM II/B-M). For mechanical performance, compressive and splitting tensile strengths increased to an optimum near 0.25% fiber before declining at 0.5%. Flexural behavior exhibited peak strength and toughness at approximately 0.25% fiber, whereas higher fiber contents primarily enhanced post-cracking ductility despite a slight reduction in total energy absorption. These results provide practical dosage guidance: fiber contents up to 0.25% ensure reliable SCC performance across cement types, while higher dosages require rheological re-optimization depending on placement constraints.

sections.heading: Background of SCC
paragraphs: The quality of the placement and compaction of concrete is the primary determinant of the concrete performance. The common defects in conventional vibrated concrete (NVC) include honeycombing, entrapped air voids, and a poor interfacial transition zone … which allow rapid ingress of aggressive agents [ 54 ,  77 ]. In Japan, self-compacting concrete (also known as self-consolidating concrete in North America) was developed in the late 1980s to early 1990s with the objective of both achieving free-flowing concrete under its own weight, fulfilling complex formwork, and non-segregated concrete [ 77 ]. SCC has been categorized as a family of engineered concretes since its rapid adoption in the world during the 1990s and early 2000s, which requires them to fulfill simultaneous filling, passing, and segregation resistance requirements [ 26 ,  54 ]. Such technology does not require any labor-intensive and noisy vibrations, making quality control and constructability much more achievable in congested reinforcement zones or inaccessible areas where internal vibrators cannot be used [ 26 ,  54 ,  77 ,  100 ]. Furthermore, SCC enhances building finishes and allows the use of additional cementitious materials (SCM) to be used to make it sustainable [ 17 ,  90 ]. SCC exhibits high workability characterized by low yield stress to promote flow and high plastic viscosity to prevent bleeding. The interaction dynamics of particles, aggregate content, and thixotropy control the whole rheological behavior [ 87 ,  111 ]. SCC can exhibit nonlinear behavior of shear-thickening and this is what makes SCC distinct to simply more fluid NVC [ 33 ]. Performance assessment is based on slump‑flow tests, passing ability and stability and plastic settlement should be applied to reduce local defects [ 26 ,  100 ]. Mix proportioning will therefore balance the paste volume, aggregate grading as well as the admixtures like limestone filler or viscosity modifiers to obtain the required deformability and packing [ 16 ,  18 ,  103 ].

With regards to structural performance, SCC achieves mechanical performance of compressive strength, tensile strength and elastic modulus which are similar to other conventional vibrated concrete (NVC); but, which are largely controlled by the water-binder ratio, the curing regime and type of aggregate [ 27 ,  57 ,  82 ]. Self‑compaction (or Proper consolidation) improves the achieved strength, but due to the large paste volume and powder-rich composition that are characteristic of SCC, higher volumes of supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) such as fly ash can be incorporated without losing fresh‑state workability, although it has to be carefully tuned to maintain early-age strength [ 17 ,  90 ,  117 ]. The lower coarse aggregate content characteristic of SCC makes it more susceptible to shrinkage and creep than NVC, which means that SCC needs mitigation options like optimized packing and controlled ratios of water to powder to minimize the cracking potential ([ 62 ,  82 ,  94 ,  103 ]. The excellent homogeneity and reduced placement losses inherently determine the durability of SCC; when the pore structure is properly designed, the transport and chloride resistance is similarly competitive with vibrated concrete ([ 83 ,  93 ,  116 ]. However, durability is not an automatic consequence of self-compaction and must be verified through transport testing, especially when using varying fillers or SCMs [ 52 ,  90 ]. Today, SCC is standard for heavily reinforced walls, complex precast elements, and retrofit projects where production speed and surface finish are the predominant factors [ 26 ]. Full-scale studies confirm that stable SCC mixtures can achieve uniform in-situ properties comparable to properly compacted NVC, making its value proposition a balance of reduced quality risk and improved productivity against the need for rigorous control over materials variability, rheology, and formwork pressure [ 26 ,  52 ,  87 ,  117 ].

sections.heading: Code criteria of SCC
paragraphs: Concrete is classified as self-compacting concrete (SCC) when its fresh state simultaneously satisfies filling ability to spread and fill formwork under its own weight, passing ability to flow through congested reinforcement without blocking, and segregation resistance to remain homogeneous during flow and rest [ 26 ,  54 ,  77 ]. Filling ability is quantified using slump-flow diameter and t 500  time, often complemented by V-funnel time to reflect viscosity [ 54 ,  100 ]. Passing ability is assessed through obstruction tests like the L-box test (H2 over H1 ratio) or J-ring, while segregation resistance is evaluated via sieve segregation indices, settlement-based indices, and visual stability assessments [ 1 ,  54 ,  77 ,  87 ]. SCC acceptance is fresh-performance-based rather than strength-based, meaning no universal strength threshold defines it [ 27 ]. However, fiber-reinforced SCC specifications often include flexural toughness and residual capacity requirements like post-cracking response [ 59 ,  113 ]. The specific acceptance ranges for the key fresh-property tests; t 500 , slump-flow diameter, V-funnel time, L-box ratio, and visual segregation resistance and how they differ across EN 12350, ACI 237R-07, and JSCE are summarized in Table  1 .

sections.heading: Materials selection and proportioning considerations for SCC
paragraphs: Published mix-design approaches for self-compacting concrete (SCC) do not fix the cement-to-fine aggregate (C/FA) proportion by a single code requirement, but the ratio converges to a narrow practical band to mobilize a lubricating mortar phase while maintaining a stable aggregate proportion. In medium-to-high strength mixes, cement contents commonly fall within the 350–480 kg/m³ range and are paired with roughly 750–1050 kg/m³ of fine aggregate, implying a typical C/FA by mass on the order of 0.35–0.60 depending on the use of fillers like limestone powder and supplementary cementitious materials such as fly ash or slag [ 16 ,  17 – 18 ,  24 ,  99 ,  103 ]. This structural design intentionally reduces coarse aggregate dominance to increase mortar volume and powder fineness, securing deformation capacity and robustness in confined reinforcement [ 27 ,  54 ,  77 ]. Classical Japanese and packing-based approaches often start near a 0.50 sand fraction, meaning sand and gravel are each about half as a practical starting point for packing and passing [ 18 ,  103 ]. In practice, the fine aggregate to total aggregate ratio generally ranges from 48 to 57% for SCC, with EFNARC guidance placing common sand fractions around 0.48–0.55 to balance passing ability and segregation resistance [ 29 ,  61 ]. Packing-factor optimization studies show that the best sand share can shift upward to 0.57 when aggregate packing density, paste volume, and fiber-induced blocking risk are considered [ 35 ]. Ultimately, SCC performance relies on a tuned balance among powder content, a sand-rich aggregate skeleton, and rheology control.

Despite its placement advantages, SCC has inherent limitations related to its mixture composition. The large paste fraction and low content of coarse aggregate result in an increase in drying shrinkage and a tendency for restrained shrinkage cracking especially in members with high surface to volume ratio [ 45 ,  58 ,  78 ]. Also, SCC can exhibit elevated creep responsiveness compared to conventional vibrated concrete, which is critical for long‑span or flexural members [ 57 ,  63 ]. Fresh‑state performance is highly sensitive to variations in moisture content, aggregate grading, and admixture compatibility; small changes can cause blocking or segregation [ 16 ,  27 ,  54 ]. Although durability is normally high, it is controlled by binder chemistry, refinement of the pore, and the capacity to manage cracks [ 25 ,  116 ]. Nylon fiber (NF) helps to overcome these weaknesses by offering crack-bridging and post-cracking load-transfer system [ 118 ]. Empirical studies of nylon-fiber-modified SCC show that fresh properties tend to exhibit reduced slump flow and increased blocking sensitivity, but hardened behavior is characterized by an increase in its resistance to cracking and energy absorption [ 56 ,  86 ,  101 ]. In order to maintain passability and avoid balling of fibers, most studies limit NF to the range of micro to low macro typically analyzing volume fractions of fibers between 0 and 0.5% [ 56 ,  86 ]. Longer fibers also provide excellent bridging and flexural toughness but at the cost of reduced workability, whilst shorter fibers made of micro nylon are more efficient in controlling plastic shrinkage, at the cost of a smaller workability reduction [ 56 ,  86 ,  101 ,  118 ]. Polymeric nature of nylon facilitates cohesion but increases yield stress and plastic viscosity; these factors have to be controlled to ensure sufficient filling capacity [ 54 ,  56 ]. Nylon fibers provide several advantages in cementitious composites. Their high tensile strength of approximately 900 MPa and relatively large elongation capacity allow significant energy dissipation through fiber pull-out, improving post-cracking ductility and crack resistance [ 85 ,  101 ]. Unlike steel fibers, nylon is non-corrosive and chemically stable under normal cementitious environments, while also providing effective control of plastic and drying shrinkage cracks [ 3 ,  101 ]. In SCC, distributed nylon fibers can improve cohesion, reduce bleed-water migration, and enhance segregation resistance in paste-rich mixtures [ 56 ]. However, nylon possesses a relatively low elastic modulus of about 5 GPa compared with hardened cement paste, limiting its contribution to pre-cracking stiffness and structural tensile capacity [ 34 ,  118 ]. The fiber-matrix bond is governed primarily by mechanical anchorage and friction because the hydrophobic fiber surface limits direct chemical interaction with hydration products [ 102 ]. At excessive dosages, fiber agglomeration or balling may occur, creating voids and increasing porosity, which can adversely affect mechanical performance and workability [ 85 ]. Therefore, the effectiveness of nylon fibers is strongly dependent on achieving an optimum dosage that balances fresh-state performance with crack-bridging and toughness enhancement.

Regarding cement systems, Portland cement (CEM I) is clinker-dominant and provides strong early hydration heat and strength, whereas CEM II/A-M and CEM II/B-M are Portland-composite cements with lower clinker fractions. The A and B designations indicate increasing proportions of non-clinker constituents, with CEM II/B-M containing more supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) or fillers (EN 197-1). These blended systems alter hydration kinetics: Limestone accelerates early hydration through nucleation … slag improves later‑age microstructure densification, and fly ash improves packing and long-term pozzolanic refinement [ 15 ,  64 ,  71 ,  81 ,  95 ]). In SCC, these effects translate into improved fresh workability and stability due to better particle packing, although early strength development may be slower [ 17 ,  18 ,  24 ,  41 ,  99 ]. Higher-SCM composite cements may struggle to reach self-compacting criteria without careful admixture control [ 25 ,  54 ]. Moving from OPC to higher composite cement content can enhance flow robustness and segregation resistance, with compressive strength recovering or improving at later ages depending on SCM type and curing [ 25 ,  41 ,  64 ,  116 ]. sections.heading: Research significance
paragraphs: In Bangladesh, routine concrete construction increasingly utilizes Portland composite cements manufactured as CEM II/A-M and CEM II/B-M, while ordinary Portland cement constitutes only a small share of national consumption according to the Bangladesh Cement Manufacturers Association [ 12 ,  60 ]). These cements incorporate fly ash, slag, and limestone to reduce clinker content, which is significant for sustainability because the industry contributes 7–8% of global anthropogenic CO₂ emissions, with clinker production being the dominant source [ 11 ,  43 ,  46 ,  51 ]. Utilizing supplementary cementitious materials is recognized as one of the most effective short- to medium-term strategies for lowering the carbon footprint of construction [ 92 ].

Self-compacting concrete (SCC) is uniquely sensitive to binder composition and fines affecting fresh rheology, so trends from ordinary Portland cement systems cannot be extrapolated to SCC using local cements with varying proportions of fly ash, slag, and limestone [ 77 ]. With regard to cement systems, Portland cement (CEM I) is mainly clinker-based, which provides high early hydration heat and rapid strength development, whereas CEM II/A-M and CEM II/B-M are Portland cement composite cements gaining less and less clinker content. The A and B qualifiers represent more and more proportions of non-clinker components, whereby CEM II/B-M uses more substitutions of supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) or fillers according to EN 197-1. These mixed systems alter hydration kinetics: Early reactions are accelerated by limestone via nucleation and carboaluminate pastes, later reactions are catalyzed by slag via densification, and the efficiency of packing is promoted by fly ash via long-term refinement of pozzolana [ 15 ,  64 ,  71 ,  81 ,  95 ]. Therefore, a systematic evaluation of SCC based on Bangladesh-specific Type II composite cements would be justified whereby fresh-state acceptability and mechanical performance are important. Besides that, nylon or polyamide fibers can be added to suppress the crack and flexural toughness but can only be used with care since it can hinder flow and passage of SCC [ 9 ,  113 ]. Setting the optimum level of nylon fibers that meet the requirements of fresh state and improves mechanical behavior defines an issue of high practical importance. Finally, this study combines the material availability, structural performance and sustainability into consideration in order to provide evidence-based mix-design advice to Bangladeshi construction industry.

sections.heading: Mix design philosophy and method selection
paragraphs: The SCC mix design framework used in this study was governed by the twin requirements to achieve stable self-spreading behavior and reliable structural performance. While the methods based on particle packing provide a hard theoretical base, their implementation in practice requires the exhausting characterization of the size distribution of particles and the optimization of the packing density - a task which proves untenable in the light of local laboratory and field constraints.

An empirical mix design approach was therefore taken. This methodology has widespread application in SCC research and practice, especially when locally-sourced material is used. It allows a systematic regulation of the water/binder ratio, paste volume, aggregate proportion and admixture dosage, whilst maintaining a sufficient flexibility for performance driven optimization. Moreover, the empirical framework allows the direct evaluation of the level of interdependence between the fresh and hardened properties which is at the heart of SCC behavior.

Initial SCC proportions were established from published SCC mix-design ranges and then calibrated using local materials through four OPC-based trial mixtures (Mixes M1–M4). The trials differed primarily in the sand/total aggregate ratio (S/A) to bracket commonly reported SCC aggregate windows, namely 57.10%, 50.70%, 48.10%, and 53.30%, respectively. Minor adjustments were also made to the water-to-cement ratio, coarse aggregate content, and superplasticizer dosage to obtain a balanced combination of flowability, passing ability, and stability. These parameters were modified together because SCC performance is governed by their combined interaction rather than by any single constituent. The trial mixtures were therefore intended to progressively refine the mixture proportions using locally available materials until the SCC acceptance criteria were satisfied, rather than to evaluate the isolated effect of individual mix parameters. Each trial mix was evaluated against SCC fresh-property acceptance requirements for filling ability, passing ability, and segregation resistance, with target performance broadly consistent with SF2 slump-flow and moderate viscosity (VF1) classifications, and checked against guidance in EN 12350, ACI 237R-07, and JSCE recommendations. The mix that consistently satisfied the full set of fresh-performance criteria was selected as the baseline proportion (Mix M4) for the main experimental matrix.

sections.heading: Identification of samples and process flow
paragraphs: Using this baseline, the study investigated the combined influence of locally available composite cement and nylon fiber reinforcement. Two cement types, CEM II/A-M (AM) and CEM II/B-M (BM) were used, each combined with four nylon fiber volume fractions (0, 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5% by total concrete volume), yielding eight final mixtures. Mixtures were coded as M#CEMfX%, where M# denotes the selected trial mix number, CEM is omitted for OPC or written as AM or BM, and fX% indicates fiber dosage; for example, M4BMf0.1% denotes trial Mix 4 proportions with CEM II/B-M and 0.1% nylon fiber. The process flow diagram of the research is illustrated in Fig.  1 .

sections.heading: Cement
paragraphs: Three types of cement were used as primary bonding material.

Ordinary Portland Cement (CEM-I) of 52.5 N grade cement was used with specific gravity of 3.15. Portland Composite Cement (CEM-II/A-M) of strength class 42.5 N was used which contains: Clinker-80–94%; Fly ash, Slag and Limestone: 6–20%; Gypsum: 0–5%. Portland Composite Cement (CEM-II/BM) of strength class 42.5 N was used which contains: Clinker: 65–79%; Fly ash, slag and Limestone-21–35%; Gypsum-0–5%.

sections.heading: Nylon fiber
paragraphs: Nylon fiber is a synthetic polyamide fiber widely used as secondary reinforcement in cementitious composites. It is valued for its high tensile strength, abrasion resistance, and good chemical stability, and it exhibits relatively low moisture absorption compared to many natural fibers. When incorporated into concrete at appropriate dosages, nylon fibers primarily enhance crack control and post-cracking load transfer, helping to improve ductility and toughness rather than acting as a direct substitute for conventional steel reinforcement. The properties of nylon fibers are shown in Table  5 . Some sample of nylon fiber is shown in Fig.  4 .
Table 5 Properties of nylon fiber Material Specific weight Elastic modulus (GPa) Tensile strength (MPa) Melting point (°C) Chemical resistance Size (mm) Nylon fiber 1.14 5.17 896 225 Good 25
Fig. 4 25 mm size nylon fiber

A fiber length of 25 mm was selected based on evidence from comparative studies examining nylon fibers of 19, 25, and 50 mm in concrete. At 25 mm, the fiber-to-maximum aggregate size ratio is approximately 1.7 relative to the 19 mm nominal aggregate used in this study, which falls within the range recommended to avoid inter-fiber mechanical interlocking and aggregate blocking at confined flow paths such as the L-box and V-funnel openings [ 56 ,  85 ]. Studies on nylon fiber aspect ratio report that peak splitting tensile and flexural strengths both are achieved with a fiber length of 25 mm, whereas the 50 mm length produces disproportionate workability penalties in SCC without commensurate strength gain [ 102 ]. The 25 mm length thus represents a practical compromise: it is long enough to bridge macro-cracks effectively under flexural loading, yet short enough to remain dispersible at the fiber dosages (0–0.5%) investigated in this study.

sections.heading: Superplasticizer
paragraphs: Auramix 300 was used as superplasticizer which is a high-performance retarding agent based on a poly carboxylic ether polymer with long lateral chains. The volumetric mass of this superplasticizer at 200 °C is 1.085 kg/liter with a pH value of minimum 6.

sections.heading: Mix proportions
paragraphs: Phase One established an OPC-based SCC baseline by preparing four trial mixes (M1–M4) with systematic variations in water–cement ratio, aggregate proportions, and superplasticizer dosage. The mixture proportions were selected to evaluate combinations capable of achieving the fundamental SCC requirements of filling ability, passing ability, and segregation resistance while remaining compatible with the locally sourced materials used in this study. The sand-to-total aggregate ratio was varied between 48.1 and 57.1% to provide different levels of mortar volume and aggregate packing, whereas the water–cement ratio was adjusted between 0.37 and 0.53 to investigate a practical range of workability and strength characteristics. Superplasticizer dosage was modified as required to promote self-compaction while maintaining mixture stability and cohesion. Collectively, these variations were intended to identify a mixture proportion capable of satisfying SCC performance requirements while providing adequate compressive, tensile, and flexural properties for subsequent evaluation of cement type and nylon fiber content. The trial mixes were assessed using a multi-criteria acceptance framework, where a mix was considered satisfactory only if it met SCC requirements for filling ability, passing ability, and segregation resistance collectively; mixtures showing segregation, excessive flow with inadequate cohesion, or blockage risk were rejected even when individual test outcomes appeared acceptable.

The fresh-state acceptance of SCC was judged by a common performance envelope, not by a single code. When EN 12350, ACI 237R-07, and JSCE gave different limits, the most restrictive limit was used as the governing criterion. This is consistent with SCC practice, because SCC is defined by filling ability, passing ability, and segregation resistance, while the exact numerical ranges vary by standard. The same rule was applied to select the baseline mix and to compare all cement and fiber combinations. Based on the fresh-property evaluation (test results are detailed in Sect.  3 ), Mix Design 4 (M4) demonstrated the most consistent compliance across the SCC criteria and was therefore selected as the reference proportion for the subsequent phase involving cement-type variation (CEM II/A-M and CEM II/B-M) and nylon fiber contents (0–0.5% by cement mass). The mixture proportions of the OPC trial mixes used for SCC selection are presented in Table  6 , while the proportions of the final composite-cement and nylon-fiber SCC mixtures are summarized in Table  7 .

sections.heading: Fresh property evaluation
paragraphs: Fresh mix properties were studied to determine the rheological stability, flowability, and passing capacity of the SCC mixtures under gravity driven placement. The evaluative protocol followed the guidelines set out by EN 12350, ACI 237R-07, and JSCE which collectively define performance-based acceptance criteria for SCC without using prescriptive mix limits.

The V-Funnel, L-Box, T₅₀₀ slump flow time, and slump flow diameter tests were used to characterize complementary aspects of SCC behavior, including viscosity-controlled flow, segregation resistance, passing ability through congested reinforcement, and free-flow deformation capability. All tests were completed within 35–40 min of mixing. No additional water was introduced after admixture dosage to prevent unintended modification of yield stress and plastic viscosity.

Since all fresh-property tests were completed within short duration after mixing, the results primarily represent the early-age workability characteristics of the SCC mixtures. It is recognized that workability retention may vary during longer placement durations in mixtures containing nylon fibers and composite cements, as ongoing hydration and fiber–matrix interactions can influence viscosity development and flow retention over time. The present study did not include extended workability-retention measurements beyond the testing window. Therefore, future investigations may evaluate the evolution of slump flow, T₅₀₀, V-funnel time, and passing ability at different elapsed times to assess the long-term rheological stability of these mixtures.

Segregation resistance was evaluated through visual stability assessment during fresh-property testing. Visual assessment is recognized in SCC practice and is incorporated in ACI 237R-07 and EFNARC guidance as a practical indicator of mixture stability [ 10 ,  29 ,  77 ]. Visual stability was evaluated using the Visual Stability Index (VSI) method (ASTM C1611/ACI 237R-07) by systematically inspecting the slump-flow patty, its peripheral edge, and the concrete surface in the mixing pan. The assessment focused on three indicators: the presence/width of a mortar ring (paste without coarse aggregate) at the edge, central accumulation of coarse aggregates, and the extent of surface bleeding. Each mixture was assigned a VSI rating from 0 (highly stable) to 3 (highly unstable) based on these observations. A rating of 0 or 1 (no mortar ring, or only minor bleeding without aggregate-paste separation) constituted a “pass”, confirming adequate segregation resistance. Conversely, a distinct mortar ring exceeding 10 mm in width, significant central aggregate pile-up, or severe visible bleeding (VSI 2–3) resulted in a “fail” by visual stability criteria. Although quantitative methods such as sieve segregation testing can provide a more detailed evaluation, these facilities were not available in the laboratory used for the present study.

sections.heading: V-Funnel flow time
L-Box passing ability
T₅₀₀ slump flow time
paragraphs: The T₅₀₀ slump flow time represents the rate of radial spread and is used as an indirect indicator of plastic viscosity. The parameter was recorded as the time required for the SCC to reach a spread diameter of 500 mm after cone lifting. Higher values indicate excessive viscosity and reduced filling ability, while very low values can correspond to unstable or segregation-prone mixes.

sections.heading: Selection of mix ratio from trial mixes
paragraphs: Fresh-state self-compacting concrete performance was investigated for four baseline mixes, identified as M1f0%, M2f0%, M3f0%, and M4f0%, using standard tests that evaluate flowability, viscosity, and passing ability, namely- slump flow diameter, t 500  time, V-funnel time, and L-box ratio. The measured values reported in Table  8  demonstrate clear differences in rheological behavior among the mixes, indicating that variations in mixture proportioning significantly influence SCC performance. When these results are assessed and compared against the acceptance limits defined in EN 12350, ACI 237R-07, and JSCE shown in Table  1 , the suitability of each mix as self-compacting concrete can be clearly differentiated. The comparison is illustrated in Fig.  6 .

Table 8 Fresh properties test results of the trial mixes Mix ID V (s) L (H2/H1) t 500  (s) Slump diameter (mm) Segregation resistance M1f0% 3.84 0.98 1.11 982.98 Could not Pass M2f0% 22.13 0.67 7.31 546.1 Could not Pass M3f0% 14.09 0.81 6.01 645.16 Passed M4f0% 12.22 0.83 5.69 662.94 Passed
Fig. 6 Comparison of fresh properties of mixes with different SCC standards

Mix M1f0% has excellent flowability, measured in terms of slump flow diameter of 982.98 mm, which exceeds upper limits defined by all three normative references. This strong deformability is accompanied by significantly low viscosity, as confirmed by V-funnel time of 3.84 s, and t 500  time of 1.11 s.—both lower than the minima. Such a profile usually predicts an increased susceptibility to segregation and instability and thus this mix is not suitable as a stable SCC reference. On the other hand, the M2f0% shows far too stiff and viscous behavior with the V-funnel time (22.13 s) and t 500  time (7.31 s) being far above the admissible upper limits. Furthermore, its L-box ratio of 0.67 implies insufficient passing capability and its slump-flow diameter of 546.1 mm is at or below the minimum requirement, thus indicating unsatisfactory self-compacting performance. Mix M3f0% shows an intermediate response with better flowability and passing ability indicated by slump-flow diameter 645.16 mm and L-box ratio 0.81, but with viscosity-related parameters still at the marginal level with V-funnel time 14.09s exceeding the EN limit and slightly above the JSCE limit. The t 500  time (6.01s) was also on the borderline of ACI and above the JSCE requirement. The segregation resistance was determined by visual observation. Mix M3f0% and M4f0% passed the test and other two formulations failed. The excessive flowability of M1f0% is related to the higher sand to total aggregate ratio (57.10%) and higher water-cement ratio (0.53), which leads to the development of excess paste that could not be adequately stabilized by the aggregate skeleton and thus leading to the segregation. Conversely, poor performance of M2f0% is due to the lower fraction of sand (50.70%) and lower water-cement ratio (0.37), which produce the inadequate mortar lubrication and excessive inter-particle friction that limit the flow and passing capability.

Among all mixes, M4f0% provides the most balanced and consistent performance because it achieved acceptable filling ability, passing ability, and stability simultaneously while remaining within the governing acceptance limits. This mix exhibits a slump flow diameter of 662.94 mm, a t 500  time of 5.69 s, an L-box ratio of 0.83, and a V-funnel time of 12.22s, collectively satisfying most of the SCC criteria across the three international standards. Using this mix as the baseline ensures that the later evaluation of cement type and nylon fiber content effects is conducted on an SCC mixture that is already compliant with fundamental performance requirements.

Since SCC is defined primarily by fresh-state performance i.e. filling ability, passing ability, and stability rather than by a single universal compressive-strength threshold, there is no fixed strength criterion that makes a concrete ‘SCC’. The required hardened strength is instead specified by the structural application requirements, while SCC-specific guidance focuses on fresh behavior [ 10 ,  29 ]. In this context, the compressive-strength results plotted against water-to-cement ratio in Fig.  7  to show the expected normal-concrete trend: strength decreases as w/c increases. Specifically, the compressive strength decreases from 5937 psi at w/c 0.37 for M2f0% to 4636 psi at w/c 0.42 for M3f0%, 3931 psi at w/c 0.46 for M4f0%, and 2643 psi at w/c 0.53 for M1f0%. This monotonic reduction is consistent with the classical Abrams’ law concept and long-established mixture-proportioning practice, where the w/c ratio is a primary parameter used to estimate and control compressive strength (ACI PRC-211.1-22; [ 44 ]. Therefore, the strength–w/c relationship observed here does not indicate any unusual hardened-state behavior attributable to the concrete being self-compacting; rather, it confirms that the mixes follow the conventional strength governing mechanism dominated by w/c, while SCC qualification is addressed separately through the fresh-property criteria [ 10 ].
Fig. 7 Compressive strength vs. water cement ratio of trial mixes

sections.heading: Comparison of SCC fresh properties
paragraphs: After selecting M4f0% as the base mix, the cement type was changed and nylon fiber was added in different content to investigate the effect of synthetic fiber content, fly ash, slag and limestone content of cement on SCC. The key outputs of fresh properties are summarized in Table  9 .

Table 9 Results of fresh properties of SCC mixes Mix ID V (s) H 2 /H 1 t  500  (s) Slump diameter (mm) Segregation resistance M4AMf0% 10.47 0.86 5.29 671.31 Passed M4AMf0.1% 10.79 0.87 5.34 651.36 Passed M4AMf0.25% 12.82 0.85 5.28 613.26 Passed M4AMf0.5% 12.93 0.83 5.58 590.56 Passed M4BMf0% 7.67 0.93 4.18 790.66 Passed M4BMf0.1% 8.69 0.92 4.34 785.02 Passed M4BMf0.25% 9.14 0.92 4.49 769.94 Passed M4BMf0.5% 9.48 0.91 4.63 753.40 Passed

The slump flow diameter decreased progressively with increasing nylon fiber content for both cement systems (Fig.  8 ). Plain SCC mix (0% fiber) achieved slump flow values ranging from 660 to 790 mm, well within SCC acceptance criteria. At 0.1% fiber addition, slump flow remained largely compliant, decreasing by approximately 10–20 mm. However, at 0.25% fiber, the reduction became more prominent, and at 0.5% fiber, the M4AM mix approached the lower acceptable limit (~ 550 mm) while M4BM maintained slightly better flowability.
Fig. 8 SCC fresh properties vs. nylon fiber content

The progressive decrease of flow is attributed to the formation of a three-dimensional network by nylon fibers within the concrete matrix which severely restricts the mobility of the paste and increases internal friction [ 3 ,  56 ]. Fibers obstruct flow paths, thereby increasing the apparent viscosity of the composite system. Furthermore, the hydrophobic surface of nylon locally affects water distribution in the paste, leading to high yield stress [ 65 ]. The t 500  time, which is the time needed to reach a 500 mm spread, showed the corresponding augmentation with the fiber dosage. Plain mixes produced t 500  value of 5.29 s for M4AM mix, which increased to 5.58 s when 0.5% fiber dosage was used. The observed trend indicates a decrease in the flow of velocity owing to an increase in internal resistance. Although the t 500  values did not show monotonic increase with the increasing fiber contents, the overall rheological behavior was consistent with that of the fiber reinforced self-compacting concrete (SCC). A similar sensitivity of t 500  to early-stage flow and fiber orientation has been reported previously [ 53 ,  91 ]. The viscosity increase of fiber results from mechanical interlocking of fiber and aggregate and dissipates kinetic energy.

Notably, the M4BM mix kept its flowability superior to M4AM at equal fiber dosages. This advantage is the result of the positive effect of a higher supplementary cementitious material (SCM) content in M4BM. The spherical shape of fly ash particles acts as a lubricating agent and hence decreases the inter-particle friction [ 8 ,  17 ]. Additionally, the higher powder volume in CEM II/B-M increases the volume and cohesiveness of the paste and enhances the suspension capability of fibers and maintenance of flow properties despite fiber addition [ 6 ]. V-funnel time showed a systematic increase with fiber content as it went from 7.7 to 10.5 s in plain mixes to 9.5–12.9 s in mixes with 0.5% fiber incorporated in the M4AM to M4BM mixes. This parameter is a measure of the ability of concrete to flow through confined spaces under the force of gravity. Fibers limit the flow through the constricted funnel hole by forming temporary blockages and increasing the apparent viscosity [ 68 ]. The M4AM system showed a higher sensitivity to fiber addition with V-funnel times to be over 12 s at 0.5% fiber - approaching the upper limit of most SCC specifications. Conversely, M4BM was able to keep V-funnel times below 10 s even at 0.5% fiber and thus had better control of viscosity. This disparity is due to improved particle packing and better rheological stability provided by the higher SCM content in CEM II/B-M which gives a more cohesive paste due to fiber-induced flow restrictions [ 25 ,  41 ].

The L- box ratio is a measure of the ability of concrete to flow through the obstacles of reinforcement bars. All fiber free mixes had excellent passing ability ranging from 0.86 to 0.93 well above the 0.80 minimum threshold. At 0.1–0.25% fiber the passing ability was still acceptable (0.85–0.92), whereas at 0.5% fiber, the M4AM mix showed slightly over the threshold value while M4BM showed better compliance. Fiber addition compromises passing ability through several mechanisms. Fibers can bridge across reinforcement bars, forming temporary blockages that cause aggregate bridging [ 37 ,  38 ]. Additionally, fiber orientation at flow fronts causes anisotropic resistance as fibers tend to align perpendicular to the flow direction near obstacles and this increases the risk of blockage [ 73 ]. As for the superior performances of M4BM at higher fiber contents, improvements in workability retention and paste volume can be attributed to maintenance of adequate lubrication of fibers and aggregates around it when passing through restricted spaces. The finer particle size distribution of high-SCM systems also enhances the ability of the matrix to transport fibers through the obstacles without segregation [ 17 ,  99 ]. Visual stability assessment confirmed that all mixes ranging from 0 to 0.5% fiber passed segregation resistance criteria. This suggests that although flowability is reduced with increasing fiber dosages, the mixes have maintained sufficient cohesiveness to avoid aggregate separation. Nylon fibers have the ability to improve the segregation resistance by providing a reinforcing structure that helps to limit aggregate movement and increase the cohesion of the paste [ 3 ].

Comparing the measured fresh properties to the standards EN 12350, ACI 237R-07 and JSCE shows that the compliance of SCC depends on fiber dosage. All mixes at 0 and 0.1 per cent fiber met the full set of SCC criteria in all three standards. At 0.25 per cent fiber, both cement systems were stillmostly compliant, though nearing extremities in some parameters. At the level of 0.5% fiber, M4AM showed marginal or non-compliant behavior in several criteria (slump flow, V-funnel, and L-box), whereas M4BM was still borderline acceptable for this mix proportion. This performance hierarchy allows us to set dosage limits for fibers that can be incorporated into both cement systems in practice: a dosage of up to 0.25 per cent of fibers can be safely used and both cement systems will still assure reliable SCC behavior, 0.5 per cent fiber can approach or exceed limits for workability in the case of M4AM but is passable for M4BM, where improved flow and passing ability justifies attention to quality control. Beyond 0.5% fiber, major mixture modifications (increased superplasticizer dosage, aggregate proportions, or other powder content) would be necessary to restore the compliance of SCC properties [ 30 ,  56 ]). The fresh-property results highlight the fundamental trade-off in fiber-reinforced SCC: improved crack control and toughness come at the expense of reduced flowability and passing ability. Achieving an optimal balance therefore depends on selecting the fiber dosage in relation to cement type and placement requirements, with high-SCM cements such as CEM II/B-M showing greater tolerance for fiber incorporation while still maintaining self-compacting characteristics.

sections.heading: Compressive and tensile strength
paragraphs: After testing the result of compressive and tensile strength of the samples are shown in Table  10 . Figure  9  shows the effect of nylon fiber content on the compressive and split tensile strength at 28 days of SCC prepared with CEM II/A-M (M4AM) and CEM II/B-M (M4BM) cements. Both cement systems show a non-monotonic behavior to the addition of fibers, showing an early increase in strength up to an optimum fiber dosage and a decrease with increasing fiber contents.

Table 10 Results of compressive and tensile strength test Mix ID Compressive strength (psi) SD (psi) CoV Tensile strength (psi) SD (psi) CoV M4AMf0% 3349 119 3.55 721 29 4.02 M4AMf0.1% 3460 165 4.77 840 12 1.43 M4AMf0.25% 3930 103 2.62 950 36 3.79 M4AMf0.5% 3501 66 1.89 859 18 2.10 M4BMf0% 2048 122 5.96 470 29 6.17 M4BMf0.1% 2215 78 3.52 541 12 2.22 M4BMf0.25% 2415 96 3.98 680 27 3.97 M4BMf0.5% 2200 29 1.32 579 44 7.60

For compressive strength, the M4AM series shows maximum strength at around 0.25% of fiber content- 3930 psi as compared to 3349 psi for the plain mix, which is gain of about 17.36%. Beyond this optimum, there is a reduction in strength to 3501 psi at 0.5% fiber. The M4BM series has a similar pattern, but these are lower absolute values: going from 2048 psi (0% fiber) to 2415 psi (0.25% fiber) with a 17.9% increase then back to 2200 psi at 0.5%. The initial strength enhancement at low fiber dosages can be attributed to the bridging of propagating microcracks by the well-dispersed nylon fibers, which redistributes localized stresses and effectively delays the crack coalescence, thereby improving the load-bear capacity [ 101 ,  102 ]. However, too much fiber content than the optimum values bring in a conflict of detrimental effects: fiber agglomeration resulting in weak zones with insufficient paste encapsulation, air voids resulting in increased porosity, and a decrease in the workability in the mixing stage resulting in non-uniform distribution of fibers [ 3 ,  85 ]. These defects outweigh the benefits of crack bridging and lead to net reduction in strength. The consistently lower compressive strength of M4BM compared to M4AM is attributed to its lower clinker content and slower pozzolanic reaction kinetics of the higher SCM system at 28 days, as CEM II/B-M has 21–35% supplementary materials in comparison to 6–20% in CEM II/A-M [ 64 ,  88 ]. The lower strength of CEM II/B-M mixtures can be attributed to the reduced clinker content and higher proportion of SCM/filler constituents. Since CEM II/B-M may contain up to 35% non-clinker material, the early-to-medium age strength development at 28 days can be slower than OPC or CEM II/A-M. The lower clinker fraction reduces the amount of primary hydration products formed within the 28-day curing period, while fly ash and other SCMs generally contribute more gradually through secondary reactions. Therefore, although CEM II/B-M improved fresh SCC workability, its mixture proportions would require further optimization when higher compressive strength is required. Theachieved CEM II/B-M strengths may be suitable for low-strength or non-critical applications, but they may not be adequate for general structural members without further mix optimization.
Fig. 9 Compressive and tensile strength vs. nylon fiber percentage

Tensile strength has a greater extent of improvement with the addition of fiber as compared to compressive strength. For M4AM, the tensile strength is significantly increased (31.94%) from the plain mix to 0.25% fiber addition indicating the effectiveness of nylon fibers in crack-bridging under tensile loading. Similarly, M4BM exhibits progressive tensile improvements up to 44.68% at 0.25 fiber content before reaching a plateau. The superior tensile response is due to the direct interception of tensile cracks by nylon fibers and the transfer of stress across the crack faces by mechanical anchorage and friction, which give post-cracking load carrying capacity to the concrete structure that is completely absent in plain concrete [ 3 ,  91 ]. Even at dosages where compressive strength starts to decrease, tensile strength often remains high due to the continued function of residual fiber bridging even if individual fibers become locally clustered. The optimum fiber content observed is consistent with the literature using different mix proportions by Ahmad et al. [ 3 ] for maximum splitting tensile enhancement at 1.5% nylon fiber; and 1% identified by Monika et al. [ 72 ] for balanced mechanical performance. The cement type effect is secondary: although M4BM shows relatively lower early age hydration and consequently lower ultimate tensile strength than M4AM. The response of the two systems to the fiber reinforcement is similar in relative terms, implying that the fiber-matrix interaction mechanism is more common to the two systems and is governed by the fiber characteristics rather than by relatively small differences in the paste composition of the two binder systems tested.

sections.heading: Flexural behavior
paragraphs: The load-deflection characteristics shown in Fig.  10  show the change in flexural behavior with the increase of nylon fiber content from 0 to 0.5% in both M4AM and M4BM cement systems. Plain concrete beams (0% fiber) have the typical brittle response of an essentially linear increase of load to peak followed by sudden drop off of load and little residual capacity after initial cracking. This is due to the lack of crack-bridging mechanisms in the unreinforced cementitious matrix.
Fig. 10 Load-deflection curve at different nylon fiber percentages

The addition of fiber fundamentally changes the post peak behavior. At 0.1% fiber, the curves are beginning to display a more gradual post peak descent than sudden collapse, indicating that fibers are intercepting the primary flexural crack and maintaining partial load transfer. At 0.25% this effect is more pronounced: peak loads are increased extremely (45–60%), and the post peak level is much longer, which shows improved ductility and energy absorption capability. The mechanism that controls this response is that the nylon fibers cross the crack plane and resist crack opening through debonding and progressive pull-out from the surrounding matrix [ 13 ,  84 ]. Since nylon has elasticity modulus (5.17 GPa) and elongation that are relatively low compared to steel, during fiber pull‑out, nylon fibers undergo large deformation rather than rupturing. This allows energy dissipation for large deflections and generates the typical softening tail found in the curves [ 22 ,  76 ]. The incremental benefit of fiber content is evident: 0.5% fiber offers the highest post-crack load retention and deflection capacity, in line with more fibers being available to bridge the crack, delaying complete separation.

Comparing the two cement systems, M4AM generally achieves higher peak loads than M4BM at equivalent fiber dosages, reflecting its higher clinker content and superior 28-day matrix strength. However, the relative shape of the post-peak response, specifically the slope of the descending branch and the extent of the ductile plateau which appears to be similar between cements at each fiber level, suggesting that fiber pull-out behavior is not drastically altered by the moderate differences in paste composition between CEM II/A-M and CEM II/B-M. This observation aligns with findings that fiber-matrix interfacial properties in polymer fiber systems are influenced more by fiber surface characteristics and mechanical anchorage than by subtle variations in C-S-H morphology [ 4 ,  13 ].

Figure  11  quantifies the modulus of rupture as a function of fiber content. Both cement systems show an initial increase in flexural strength with fiber addition, peaking at approximately 0.25% fiber content before declining at 0.5%. For M4AM, the peak represents 46% for CEM II AM over the plain mix, while M4BM shows a comparable more relative gain (62%) despite lower absolute values. The first enhancement in strength results from the fibers delaying crack initiation by redistributing tensile stresses at the microscale level while the greater fiber surface area at moderate dosages results in increased potential bridging sites per unit volume [ 32 ,  101 ]. However, the later decrease at 0.5% fiber is related to the same workability-related defects that are seen in the compressive test such as fiber balling, poor compaction and higher porosity result in weak areas which can lower the effective load-bearing cross-section [ 85 ,  110 ]. The observed optimum around 0.25–0.5% fiber by cement weight (around 0.1–0.2% by the volume of concrete) is comparable to literature recommendations for nylon fiber in concrete more than this range without proportioning adjustments can generally have diminishing/negative returns [ 9 ,  32 ].
Fig. 11 Effect of nylon fiber content on flexural Strength

The slightly different response observed at 0.1% fiber may be attributed to the sensitivity of flexural strength to local fiber distribution and crack location. At low fiber dosage, only a limited number of fibers are available to bridge the critical crack plane. Therefore, a small variation in fiber orientation or dispersion within the beam can noticeably affect the measured peak flexural load. In this condition, the stronger matrix of M4AM may have provided a higher initial resistance to crack formation, while the beneficial effect of the higher SCM content in M4BM became more evident at higher fiber contents where more fibers were available for crack bridging.

Flexural toughness, quantified as the area under the load-deflection curve up to a specified deflection, shows a markedly different trend from peak strength (Fig.  12 ). Toughness generally increases with fiber content for both cement systems, with the most substantial gains occurring between 0 and 0.25% fiber, followed by a slight reduction at 0.5%. Unlike flexural strength, which is governed primarily by the peak load at crack initiation, toughness depends on the total energy absorbed throughout both the pre-cracking and post-cracking stages. Consequently, a mixture may exhibit a higher flexural strength without showing a proportional increase in toughness. Therefore, the differences observed between the flexural strength and toughness trends in the present study do not indicate inconsistency in the experimental results but rather reflect the fundamentally different mechanisms governing peak load resistance and post-cracking energy absorption. At low fiber dosages such as 0.1%, only a limited number of fibers are available to bridge the critical crack plane. In this condition, local variations in fiber distribution,orientation, and crack location can influence the post-cracking response, leading to minor fluctuations in toughness development. The slight reduction observed for the M4AM mixture at 0.1% fiber content is therefore attributed to the limited effectiveness of crack-bridging at this dosage and the inherent variability associated with a small number of fibers crossing the fracture plane. As the fiber content increases to 0.25%, the number of fibers available for crack bridging increases substantially, allowing a larger proportion of fibers to engage in pull-out and stress transfer after cracking. This results in a more effective crack-arrest mechanism and a correspondingly steeper increase in toughness. Even when peak strength begins to plateau or decrease slightly due to fiber-induced defects such as agglomeration and increased porosity, the extended post-crack load-carrying capacity and ductility provided by fiber pull-out continue to contribute significantly to the total energy absorption [ 19 ,  55 ]. At 0.25% fiber, toughness values are several times higher than the plain mix, reflecting the cumulative effect of numerous fibers engaging sequentially as the crack widens. This behavior is consistent with reports that synthetic fibers can increase fracture energy by an order of magnitude at dosages around 1–2% by volume [ 2 ,  74 ]. The cement type effect on toughness is modest: M4BM and M4AM exhibit similar relative toughness enhancement factors, suggesting that the energy dissipation mechanism governed primarily by fiber pull-out work is relatively insensitive to the paste-strength differences between these two composite cements. The practical implication is that nylon fiber is most valuable for applications prioritizing ductility and crack control rather than peak load capacity, and that dosages up to 0.5% by cement weight can provide substantial toughness enhancement even when strength gains have begun to diminish [ 84 ,  85 ].
Fig. 12 Effect of nylon fiber content on flexural toughness

sections.heading: Effect of cement types on SCC properties
paragraphs: Three fiber-free mixes, M4f0% (OPC), M4AMf0% (CEM II/A-M), and M4BMf0% (CEM II/B-M) were prepared with identical proportions to isolate the effect of binder composition on SCC fresh and hardened performance. The key compositional distinction lies in clinker fraction and supplementary cementitious material (SCM) content: OPC contains approximately 95% clinker, CEM II/A-M contains 80–94% clinker with 6–20% SCMs (fly ash, slag, limestone), and CEM II/B-M contains 65–79% clinker with 21–35% SCMs.

Figure  13  shows that cement type significantly affects the fresh-state behavior of SCC, even though the w/c ratio (0.46) and superplasticizer dosage were kept constant. M4BMf0% exhibited the most favorable rheological performance, with a slump flow of 790.66 mm, V-funnel time of 7.67 s, T₅₀₀ of 4.19 s, and L-box ratio of 0.93, indicating superior flowability, moderate viscosity, and passing ability. Although the slump flow slightly exceeded the upper limit specified by JSCE (750 mm), the mixture satisfied the corresponding EN 12350 and ACI 237R-07 acceptance ranges and demonstrated the best overall fresh-state performance among the three cement systems. M4AMf0% showed intermediate performance (671.31 mm slump flow, 10.47 s V-funnel time, 5.29 s T₅₀₀, and 0.86 L-box ratio), while M4f0% (OPC) exhibited the most restricted flow characteristics, with a slump flow of 662.94 mm, V-funnel time of 12.22 s, T₅₀₀ of 5.69 s, and L-box ratio of 0.83. This ranking, namely M4BM > M4AM > OPC, indicates the successive improvement of rheological performance with increasing SCM content. The enhanced flowability of composite cements is a result of three synergistic mechanisms: (1) spherical fly ash particles reduce inter-particle friction due to the ball-bearing effect and lower the water requirement to achieve the same fluidity [ 17 ,  99 ]), (2) fine slag particles improve particle size distribution and packing efficiency to fill the voids among larger cement particles and enhance the cohesiveness of the paste without excessive viscosity [ 41 ,  109 ]. On the contrary, the fast hydration kinetics of OPC produce a more intensive early thixotropic structure formation and higher apparent yield stress, limiting the flow and increasing the test time for viscosity-related parameters [ 70 ,  80 ,  112 ,  116 ].
Fig. 13 Effect of cement types on SCC fresh properties

Figure  14  reveals the expected strength hierarchy at 28 days: OPC achieves 3930.56 psi (27.1 MPa) compressive strength, CEM II/A-M reaches 3349.28 psi (23.1 MPa), and CEM II/B-M attains 2048.30 psi (14.1 MPa), representing approximately 85% and 52% of OPC strength respectively. This progressive reduction correlates directly with decreasing clinker content and increasing SCM replacement. The strength deficit at 28 days is primarily kinetic rather than thermodynamic: lower clinker fraction means fewer rapidly hydrating alite (C₃S) and belite (C₂S) phases available for early-age C–S–H gel formation, while fly ash remains largely unreacted. Slag’s hydraulic activity, though faster than fly ash, still proceeds more slowly than Portland cement clinker [ 64 ,  79 ,  88 ]. At moderate SCM levels (CEM II/A-M with 6–20% replacement), limestone filler can partially offset strength loss through nucleation effects that accelerate cement hydration and improve packing, while slag begins contributing hydraulic reactivity, collectively maintaining about 85% of OPC strength [ 15 ,  71 ]. At higher SCM levels (CEM II/B-M with 21–35% replacement), the dilution effect dominates and the slower pozzolanic reactions of fly ash have not yet produced substantial secondary C–S–H, resulting in the observed 48% strength reduction [ 90 ,  115 ]. Split tensile strength follows the same ranking with smaller percentage differences, as tensile capacity is more sensitive to Interfacial Transition Zone (ITZ) refinement, and SCMs can partially compensate for reduced bulk paste strength through improved paste-aggregate bonding [ 88 ,  97 ]. Critically, this 28-day snapshot does not represent ultimate performance: fly ash pozzolanic reactions intensify between 28 and 90 days, slag continues hydraulic hardening, and both SCMs densify the microstructure through secondary C–S–H formation and portlandite consumption, such that by 56–90 days CEM II systems typically match or exceed OPC strength while offering superior long-term durability [ 49 ,  66 ,  69 ].
Fig. 14 Effect of cement types on mechanical strength of SCC

Figure  15  presents flexural load-deflection responses for the three cement types without fiber reinforcement. All mixes exhibit predominantly brittle behavior characteristic of plain concrete: linear-elastic loading to peak followed by sudden load drop upon crack formation. However, subtle but meaningful differences emerge in peak load magnitude and pre-peak deflection capacity. Rapid hydration of OPC releases high early heat, creating temperature gradients that induce autogenous microcracking in the paste and weak ITZ zones where existing microcracks impair effective stress redistribution capacity and cause preferential crack initiation sites [ 105 ,  106 ]. On the other hand, CEM II/A-M and CEM II/B-M systems have a slower rate of hydration with lower peak temperatures resulting from the clinker dilution, minimizing thermal gradients and internal microcracking, leading to a more homogenous 28-day matrix with lower absolute strength [ 14 ,  98 ,  104 ]. In addition, pozzolanic reactions consume coarse portlandite crystals and replace them with fine‑grained secondary C–S–H, refining the paste microstructure and reinforcing the ITZ through improved paste-aggregate bonding and reduced interfacial porosity [ 15 ,  42 ,  95 ]. Fracture mechanics studies confirm that fly ash and slag additions increase fracture energy and critical stress intensity factor, which means that more energy is needed for crack initiation and propagation. This phenomenon leads to increased pre‑peak ductility even with lower compressive strength [ 40 ,  98 ,  114 ]. Despite these improvements, all three mixes eventually fail in a brittle manner because of the lack of crack-bridging fibers.
Fig. 15 Effect of cement types on load-deflection curve of SCC

Figure  16  demonstrates the influence of the cement type on the 28-day value of flexural strength and flexural toughness of SCC mixes. Both parameters follow the same hierarchy as the compressive strength results with the greatest values for OPC followed by CEM II/A-M and CEM II/B-M. This trend reflects the progressive decrease in clinker content and alite availability as SCM replacement level increases, which directly limits the amount of early age hydration and development of tensile resistance at 28 days [ 64 ,  96 ]. Although composite cements encourage microstructural refinement by secondary hydration reactions and better particle packing, the pozzolanic contribution between 7 and 28 days is not enough to totally compensate for the decrease of clinker content under flexural loading conditions [ 71 ,  105 ]. Limestone powder in CEM II systems enhances early hydration through nucleation effects and improves packing density; however, at higher replacement levels its dilution effect dominates, leading to reduced flexural strength compared with OPC at 28 days [ 14 ,  15 ]. A similar decreasing trend is observed for flexural toughness, as lower matrix strength and weaker paste–aggregate bonding restricts the development of wider fracture process zones and limit energy absorption during crack propagation [ 39 ,  75 ,  89 ]. These results indicate that, at 28 days, increasing SCM content in composite cements reduces both flexural strength and toughness, despite their well-documented long-term durability and later-age strength benefits [ 48 ,  67 ,  81 ,  98 ].
Fig. 16 Effect of cement types on flexural Strength and flexural toughness

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study establishes critical performance boundaries for nylon fiber–modified self-compacting concrete across three Portland cement systems commonly used in Bangladesh—OPC, CEM II/A-M, and CEM II/B-M. The findings reveal a systematic workability–toughness trade-off: increasing fiber content from 0 to 0.5% progressively reduces slump flow and passing ability while enhancing post-cracking ductility and energy absorption. Importantly, SCC compliance remained reliable up to approximately 0.25% fiber across all cement types, with higher-SCM composite cements (CEM II/B-M) demonstrating superior rheological tolerance to fiber addition due to enhanced particle packing and lubrication effects. Mechanical performance peaked near 0.25% fiber dosage, yielding 17–46% strength gains and substantial toughness improvements, whereas 0.5% fiber approached or exceeded fresh-property limits without proportional hardened-state benefits.

The practical significance lies in defining actionable fiber dosage thresholds for field implementation: up to 0.25% ensures reliable SCC behavior across cement types, while 0.5% requires rheological re-optimization depending on placement constraints. This guidance directly addresses the Bangladeshi construction sector’s reliance on composite cements (CEM II systems constitute > 80% of national production) and provides evidence-based mix-design protocols that balance sustainability, constructability, and structural performance. By demonstrating that higher-SCM cements maintain self-compacting characteristics while also accommodating fiber reinforcement, the study supports low-carbon concrete strategies without compromising fresh-state compliance.

Future research should investigate long-term durability (chloride permeability, shrinkage, creep) of these fiber-modified SCC systems beyond 28 days, optimize superplasticizer dosages for higher fiber contents (> 0.5%), and evaluate hybrid fiber combinations (nylon + steel/polypropylene) to further enhance ductility. Additionally, chemical characterization of cement types using XRF and microstructural analysis using SEM would provide valuable insights into the hydration mechanisms and fiber-matrix interfacial properties. Field-scale validation under varied curing regimes and the development of rheology-based prediction models incorporating fiber aspect ratio and cement composition would advance practical deployment in infrastructure applications.
